newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets debt stumble with Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets debt stumble with Treasuries.

text.p: Dazed by huge swings in U.S. Treasuries after the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points, emerging market debt trading practically ground to a halt, traders said.
Spreads, which had tightened slightly in anticipation of a mild "relief rally," widened or stayed at their pre-FOMC levels in sporatic trade, they said.
"We are back to the level before the announcement," said a trader.

By most accounts, the quarter-point rise in the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent had been priced into the market, but instantaneous reaction was nevertheless unsettling, the trader said, adding that he was bracing for continued turbulence ahead. "The market is very nervous," he added.
"Now that 'expectation' has become a fact," said Kip Allardt, emerging market debt strategist at CS First Boston, "a small number of people who doubted the rate rise have to act."

"The new phase for our market began three weeks ago," said a money manager, referring to the exodus of funds from emerging market bonds after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan warned of inflated asset prices during his annual testimony to Congress.
Until then, the rally in emerging markets debt was driven by global liquidty, he said. "It did not matter much what instruments you chose," he said.
The rise in U.S. rates spread fears that more rate hikes were in the offing and investors would have to be very selective in placing their bets, the manager said.
Traders said most emerging market players were sitting on fairly handsome profits and that it might take some weeks to detect their new allocation strategies.
J.P. Morgan's Emerging Market Bond Index plys (EMBI+) rose 3.36 percent year-to-date compared to a 0.07 percent decline for U.S. government securities.
"With many crossover investors, the market is very different from the days hedge funds ruled the roost," said a trader.

Michael Cembalest, vice president at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc, said the winning strategy should be built on identifying the appropriate duration and countries with the greatest potential for credit improvement.
He favored "medium" spread duration around four years, such as Venezuela DCBs and Argentina FRBs.
While Mexico Bradys have long duration, the country should be overweighted on account of its recovery momentum, he said.
Likewise, Venezuela and Peru are also countries with strengthening fundamentals, Cembalest said.
The uncertain outlook on U.S. rates has boosted options premiums.
Among the more actively traded options, the implied volatility for 30-day at-the-money option for Brazil C was quoted 18/19 percent. On the cash market, it dropped 3/8 to 77-1/4 bid.
Cash Argentina FRBs was unchanged at 90-7/8 bid, with implied volatility at 9.0 percent.
Mexico's 30-year global bond, UMS 26, fell 3/8 to 107-1/5 bid, and the implied volatility was quoted 19/20 percent.
Venesuela DCBs eased 1/8 at 87-5/8 bid and its implied volatility was quoted 15/17 percent.
